title: The C-K Team
kidRule: Right after a short vowel sound, like the I in NICKNAME, the /k/ sound is usually spelled with the team C-K, even in longer words. After a long vowel or another consonant, K works alone, as in CAKE and MILK.
hint: Listen: a short vowel sound, then '/k/' right after it. One letter is not enough here! Which two letters team up?
reminder: Right after a short vowel sound, '/k/' is spelled with the team C-K.

check.question: Why does HAMMOCK end with C-K and not just K?
check.correctAnswer: Because the '/k/' sound comes right after a short vowel sound!
distractors: Because every animal word ends in C-K
Because K is never allowed at the end of a word

words.def: A short or funny name that friends and family use instead of your real one.
words.sent: My nickname at home is Peanut.
words.story: This word began long ago as 'an ekename', which meant 'an extra name'. Over time people slid the N over, and it turned into 'a nekename'!
words.card: Uncle *Nick* has a *nickname* for every sock in his drawer!

words.def: A swinging bed made of cloth or rope that hangs between two trees or poles.
words.sent: Dad fell asleep in the hammock under the trees.
words.story: Sailors used to sleep in hammocks on ships, because a hanging bed swings gently with the waves instead of tipping the sleeper out!
words.card: A sleepy *ham* sandwich took a nap in my *hammock*!

words.def: A small jumping bug that chirps at night.
words.sent: A cricket chirped outside my window all night.
words.story: This bug chirps by rubbing its wings together, and its ears are on its front legs!
words.card: The *cricket* did a k*ick* flip on a tiny skateboard!

words.def: To try to fight or hurt someone or something.
words.sent: The kittens attack my shoelaces every morning.
words.story: Before it sprays, a skunk stamps its feet to warn other animals to back off!
words.card: The pirate sat on a *tack* and yelled, 'Pillow *attack*!'

words.def: A big bird whose tail opens into a giant fan of shiny blue and green feathers.
words.sent: The peacock spread his tail like a giant fan.
words.story: Only the male bird is called a peacock. The female is a peahen, and the babies are peachicks!
words.card: The *peacock* balanced one green *pea* on every tail feather!

words.def: A fast game where players use long sticks to knock a puck or a ball into a net.
words.sent: We play hockey on the frozen pond every winter.
words.story: Before a big ice hockey game, the pucks are kept frozen so that they slide smoothly and do not bounce!
words.card: The goalie lost his *key* inside a *hockey* net full of marshmallows!

words.def: A place where bushes and small trees grow very close together.
words.sent: A rabbit hid in the thicket until the fox went away.
words.story: Many small birds build their nests deep inside a thicket, where the tangled branches keep bigger animals out!
words.card: The *thicket* was so *thick* that the rabbit needed a map to find his own tail!

words.def: A wild dog with big pointed ears that lives in Africa and Asia.
words.sent: A jackal trotted across the dry grass at sunset.
words.story: Jackals often live in pairs. The mother and father stay together and raise their pups as a team!
words.card: *Jack* the *jackal* howled so loudly that his own ears covered themselves!

words.def: A fast ocean fish with wavy dark stripes on its shiny back.
words.sent: The fisherman caught a silver mackerel in his net.
words.story: Mackerel swim together in giant groups called schools, sometimes with thousands of fish!
words.card: *Ack*! A slippery *mackerel* is wearing my swimming goggles!

words.def: A funny poem with five lines and a bouncy rhyme.
words.sent: Grandpa made up a limerick about a goat in a boat.
words.story: Limerick is also the name of a city in Ireland! A writer named Edward Lear made these silly five-line poems famous in his 'Book of Nonsense'.
words.card: A *lime* wrote a *limerick* about a lemon who could not stop giggling!
